newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Ministers set date for choosing EMU 1st wave.
newsitem.headline: Ministers set date for choosing EMU 1st wave.

text.p: EU finance ministers on Saturday restored momentum to the bloc's bold single currency project, ironing out budget accord details and setting a date to decide on who will start off monetary union.
The 15 ministers, accompanied by European central bankers, agreed to choose the countries qualifying for the launch of EMU, due on January 1, 1999, at the end of April or early May next year.

European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy told reporters that recommendations from the European Commission and the European Monetary Institute on which states should be in the first wave of EMU would be ready by the end of March, 1998.

There would then be a period of four to five weeks for consultation with the 15 national parliaments, before finance ministers and heads of state met over a weekend to finalise the choice of who would join the euro in January 1999.
This would be at the "end of April, start of May", de Silguy said.

Officials at an informal two-day EU meeting in the Dutch coastal town of Noordwijk declined comment on speculation that the likely selection date would be Friday, May 1 1998 -- a scheduled holiday for many financial markets.

The ministers, cheered by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision to stand for re-election next year, earlier dotted the 'i's and crossed the 't's on the text of a so-called stability pact aimed at penalising governments running excessive deficits under a single currency.
Their agreement, following growing speculation on whether the single currency's launch might be delayed, gives the project fresh impetus.
Ministers agreed that governments running deficits above three percent of Gross Domestic Product would face a maximum penalty of 0.5 percent of total economic output per year.

During the first year the fine would include a fixed portion -- 0.2 percent of GDP -- and a variable portion -- an additional 0.1 percent of GDP for every percentage point the deficit exceeds the three percent threshold.
Should the offending government fail to bring its finances under control, additional fines, essentially the variable component, would be levied for every year above the target.

While the maximum annual penalty of 0.5 percent of GDP was agreed by EU leaders last December in Dublin, Saturday's deal could in practice mean a much heavier penalty if the deficit lasted for several years.
"This is an application of the Dublin agreement which reinforces the credibility of the Stability and Growth Pact," French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told a news conference.
The ministerial gathering agreed that only countries within EMU could benefit from the fines collected.

After weeks of intense speculation that the 1999 start-date might have to be delayed, Kohl's announcement coupled with recent upbeat German economic data have given ministers the chance to reaffirm a timely launch for EMU.

Uncertainty over Bonn's ability to put its public finances in order in 1997 -- the critical year for those wishing to join the single currency club -- have been primarily behind market speculation on a possible postponement.
Budget difficulties have been compounded by record unemployment in Germany and a political backdrop of widening labour unrest and public hostility to a common currency.
